title: Questions in the Temple: Tenants, Taxes, Resurrection, and Love
summary: In the temple courts Jesus tells the parable of the tenants who kill the owner's beloved son, aimed at the leaders who oppose him. He then answers a string of test questions: on paying taxes to Caesar, on the resurrection, and on the greatest commandment. He asks his own question about how the Christ can be David's son and Lord, warns against scribes who devour widows' houses, and points his disciples to a poor widow who gives everything she has.
story: The challenge to Jesus' authority at the end of chapter 11 opens a day of debate in the temple courts. One after another, the groups that held power in Jerusalem come at him: chief priests, scribes, and elders; Pharisees with the supporters of Herod; Sadducees; and a single scribe. Each tries to trap or test him, and each question reveals more about Jesus and about his questioners. By the end, verse 34 says, no one dared ask him anything more, and Jesus turns the questioning around. The chapter ends quietly with a widow and two small coins, and the next chapter begins with Jesus leaving the temple for the last time and predicting its destruction.
historical:
Several groups appear here, and they did not like each other. The chief priests, scribes, and elders made up the leadership of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council in Jerusalem. The Pharisees were a popular lay movement devoted to the law and its traditions. The Herodians were supporters of the Herod family, whose rule depended on Rome. The Sadducees were an aristocratic party closely tied to the priesthood; they held to the written law of Moses, rejected the Pharisees' oral traditions, and denied the resurrection of the dead (Acts 23:8 adds that they denied angels and spirits). Some ancient Christian writers said they accepted only the five books of Moses, though scholars debate that claim, and it may explain why Jesus answers them from Exodus.

The tax question was explosive. When Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6, a census was taken to assess a poll tax, and a Galilean named Judas led a revolt against it, arguing that paying tribute to Caesar denied God's kingship (Acts 5:37 mentions him). The tax had to be paid in Roman coin. The silver denarius of the emperor Tiberius carried his portrait and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus. To say pay would anger the crowd; to say do not pay would be sedition reported to the governor.
cultural:
Vineyards were a familiar investment. Wealthy owners, often living elsewhere, leased land to tenant farmers for a share of the harvest, and conflict between them was common. Jesus' hearers would also hear Isaiah 5:1-7, where God plants a vineyard, builds a wall, a watchtower, and a winepress, and finds only bad grapes; verse 1 echoes that description closely. Some scholars suggest the tenants assumed that, with the heir dead, land left without a claimant could be taken by those who worked it; either way, their hope is as foolish as it is violent.

The Sadducees' question rests on levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-6): if a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow so that the dead man's name would continue. The Shema, which Jesus quotes in verses 29 and 30, was Israel's central confession from Deuteronomy 6:4-5, recited by devout Jews morning and evening. The scribes' long robes marked their learning and status. The temple treasury, according to the Mishnah, included thirteen trumpet-shaped chests in the Court of the Women for offerings. The widow's two coins were the smallest in circulation, and Mark explains them for his readers in Roman terms: together they made a quadrans, a quarter of the smallest Roman copper coin.
literary: The chapter is a series of controversy dialogues of a kind common in Jewish teaching, where a question is posed, answered, and the questioner silenced. The parable of the tenants is allegorical in a way most of Jesus' parables are not: the vineyard is Israel, the owner is God, the servants are the prophets, the beloved son is Jesus, and the tenants are Israel's leaders, who know at once that the parable is about them. The questions follow a pattern: political (taxes), theological (resurrection), and moral (the greatest commandment). Then Jesus asks the question no one can answer, from Psalm 110:1, and closes with a warning and an example. The scribes who devour widows' houses (verse 40) are set directly beside a widow who gives her whole living (verse 44). The two stories are meant to be read together.

outline.t: The parable of the wicked tenants

doctrines.note: Jesus affirms the Shema: the Lord our God, the Lord is one. The most important commandment is to love this one God with every part of oneself, and the second, to love one's neighbor as oneself, flows from it. Love for God is the root and love for neighbor its necessary fruit.

Against the Sadducees Jesus affirms the resurrection of the dead. God called himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob long after their deaths, and he is not the God of the dead but of the living. The resurrection life will not simply repeat this life's arrangements; it is a new mode of life by the power of God.

Jesus presents himself as the beloved son and heir in the parable, and asks how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord. The Messiah is more than a descendant of David restored to a throne; he shares God's rule at his right hand.
The coin bears Caesar's image and belongs to him. The unspoken point is that human beings bear God's image (Genesis 1:27) and belong to God. Caesar may claim taxes; God claims the whole person.

words.note: Eikon, image or likeness. It is the word in the Greek Old Testament's version of Genesis 1:26-27, where God makes humanity in his image. Jesus' question about the image on the coin invites hearers to ask whose image they bear. Paul later calls Christ the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4, Colossians 1:15).

Agapetos, beloved. It is the word the Father's voice used at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration (1:11, 9:7). Its appearance in the parable (verse 6) makes the identification unmistakable: the one beloved son sent last of all is Jesus himself.

Agapao, to love. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew verb of Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. The love commanded here is not only feeling but whole-person devotion and action. Jesus joins two commands that were separate in the law and makes them one summary of it.

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up again. It refers to the dead being raised bodily at the end of the age, a hope expressed in Daniel 12:2 and held by the Pharisees. Jesus defends it here, and his own resurrection, predicted three times, will soon give it a first fulfillment.

christ: This chapter shows Jesus as the Son sent after the prophets, the rejected stone who becomes the cornerstone, and the Lord whom David himself worshiped. The parable foretells his death outside the vineyard and applies Psalm 118:22-23 to his vindication; the early church used the same psalm to proclaim the resurrection (Acts 4:11). Psalm 110:1, which Jesus quotes, became the Old Testament text the New Testament cites most often, because it describes the Messiah seated at God's right hand, where the risen and ascended Christ now reigns (Acts 2:34-36, Hebrews 1:13). He is also the perfect keeper of the great commandment, the one who loved God with all his heart and his neighbor as himself, and who, like the widow, will give all he has.

hard.q: Does Jesus praise the widow for giving everything, or lament a system that took her last coins?
hard.a: The traditional reading takes the story as praise: Jesus holds up the widow as a model of wholehearted giving, measured not by the amount but by the cost, and contrasts her with rich people who gave from surplus. Jesus' words, she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on, point that way, and the story fits his teaching elsewhere that God sees what others overlook. A second reading, argued by a number of modern scholars, notes that the story comes directly after Jesus condemns scribes who devour widows' houses and directly before he predicts the temple's destruction. On this view Jesus is lamenting that religious leaders allowed a poor widow to be drained of her last means of support for an institution that was about to fall. Many interpreters hold both together: Jesus honors her devotion, which is real and costly, while the context indicts a religious system that took advantage of such devotion. What the story does not do is teach that the poor should give away what they need to live, or that God's favor is bought with money.

questions: Jesus says what bears Caesar's image belongs to Caesar, and what is God's belongs to God. If you bear God's image, what does it mean for him to claim all of you?
The scribe was not far from the kingdom of God. What is the difference between agreeing with Jesus' teaching and entering the kingdom?
What would it look like for you to give out of poverty rather than surplus, whether of money, time, or attention?
